name: East-Central Tangkhul Naga
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: tang1336 is not in the catalog. The single sweep item (Blondel & Miller 2000, LSF nursery rhymes) is a Glottolog keyword artefact ('rhymes'), about French Sign Language, irrelevant, priority none. Beyond the item list, five first-hand Tangkhul phonologies on file were read (Arokianathan 1987 grammar pp.4,147; CIIL 'Tangkhul-Naga Grammar: A Study of Word Formation' e-book, mislabelled Arokianathan1987 in the sibling folder; Devi 2011 ch.II; Khuraijam 2014 ch.2; plus Gopal 2017, Matisoff 1972, Mortensen & Miller 2013, LSI 1903, the 1995 dictionary): all describe a tone language and none states a word-stress rule; Arokianathan 1987 mentions 'the stress pattern' only as a word-boundary cue. The StressTyp2 'initial stress' source, Arokianathan 1980 Tangkhul Naga Phonetic Reader, was located on Bharatavani (CIIL) but is account-gated ('Login to Read'); not on archive.org; priority high for acquisition. Haobam 2018 (Somdal phonology, Shodhganga 359825) folder exists but is empty, medium priority. S2 and OpenAlex APIs were rate-limited; Crossref title search found no Tangkhul stress/prosody titles. new_statements.rule_in_words: The only claim of a stress position is the database template: primary stress on the first syllable of every word, no secondary stress. No first-hand description states this. Every first-hand description opened (Arokianathan 1987; Victor 1997; Leisan 2016 Hunphun; Khuraijam 2014 Hundung; Devi 2011 Shangshak; Haobam 2018 Somdal; Meitei 2025 Sikibung/Kasom; Arokianathan & Sharma 1995) treats Tangkhul as a tone language (two or three lexical tones) and lists tone (plus length, nasality or juncture) as the only suprasegmentals; Arokianathan 1987 p.147 alone mentions 'the stress pattern' as a cue to word boundaries without saying where it falls.
new_statements.secondary_stress: StressTyp2 pattern 99: none (ambiguous between 'none reported' and 'verifiably none'). No primary source discusses it.
new_statements.domain_note: Database claim is word-level ('words of all sizes'); no passage, page or example in the dump. The StressTyp2 lect is labelled 'Naga' (iso NULL) and Gordon 2002 files it under 'Creole'; the identity as Tangkhul rests only on the cited source title (Arokianathan 1980 Tangkhul Naga Phonetic Reader). The first-hand tone statements are for citation-form words in the Ukhrul/Hunphun standard (Leisan 2016; Arokianathan 1987) and village lects (Hundung, Shangshak, Somdal, Sikibung, T.M. Kasom).
new_statements.identity_note: Sources cover several Tangkhul village lects: Ukhrul/Hunphun standard (Arokianathan 1987; Victor 1997; Leisan 2016; Gopal 2017; Bhat 1969; Pettigrew 1918), Hundung (Khuraijam 2014), Shangshak (Devi 2011), Somdal (Haobam 2018), Sikibung and T.M. Kasom (Meitei 2025; Kasom may belong to Southern Tangkhul khan1277). The StressTyp2 datum is filed as 'Naga' (language 241, iso NULL) and Gordon 2002 lists it under 'Creole'; it is keyed to tang1336 only through its cited source title (Arokianathan 1980 Tangkhul Naga Phonetic Reader). Glottolog's tang1336 bibliography also carries several computationally mis-assigned 'rhymes' items (Amdo Tibetan, hip-hop, LSF nursery rhymes) that are irrelevant.

new_statements.quote: There are six vowels and nineteen consonants in the language. As supra-segmental features, there are three tones, the rising, the falling, and the level. The rising (i.e., high) and the falling (i.e., low) tones are marked as /, v. respectively. The level tone is not marked. [p.4] ... The phonetic pauses, the stress pattern and the clusteral restriction, help the identification of a word in speech. [p.147]
new_statements.citation: Arokianathan, S. (1987). Tangkhul Naga Grammar. CIIL Grammar Series 16. Mysore: Central Institute of Indian Languages.
new_statements.locator: Ch. I sec. 1.1, p.4 (archive.org dli.language.2295 leaf 19); and Ch. IV sec. 4.2, p.147 (leaf 161)
new_statements.reading: The fullest first-hand description of Tangkhul by the author of the 1980 Phonetic Reader that StressTyp2 cites for 'initial stress' treats Tangkhul as a three-tone language and gives no word-stress rule at all; 'the stress pattern' appears once, as a cue for word delimitation, with no placement stated. Every other first-hand Tangkhul phonology read in this sweep (CIIL 'Study of Word Formation' e-book; Devi 2011 Shangshak; Khuraijam 2014 Hundung) likewise lists tone (with length/nasality) as the only suprasegmentals and is silent on stress. No primary source read supports a fixed-initial word-stress claim for Tangkhul; the one text that could (Arokianathan 1980 Phonetic Reader) is login-gated on Bharatavani.

sources.citation: Arokianathan, S. (1987). Tangkhul Naga Grammar. CIIL Grammar Series 16. Mysore: Central Institute of Indian Languages.
sources.quote: p.4: "There are six vowels and nineteen consonants in the language. As supra-segmental features, there are three tones, the rising, the falling, and the level. The rising (i.e., high) and the falling (i.e., low) tones are marked as /, v. respectively. The level tone is not marked." — p.147: "Word is defined by Bloomfield as a minimum meaningful unit which is a free form. The phonetic pauses, the stress pattern and the clusteral restriction, help the identification of a word in speech."
sources.locator: Ch. I Phonology sec. 1.1, p.4 (archive.org leaf 19); Ch. IV sec. 4.2 Word Formation, p.147 (leaf 161)
sources.note: Same author as the 1980 Phonetic Reader that StressTyp2 cites for 'initial stress' (lect 244 'Naga'). The grammar lists tone as the only suprasegmental feature and states no stress rule; 'the stress pattern' is mentioned once, as a cue for delimiting words, with no placement given. Silent on where stress falls.
